ubermensch: The Übermensch, or "overman," is Friedrich Nietzsche's image of a human being who creates values out of their own strength rather than inheriting them from tradition, religion, or the crowd. Introduced in Thus Spoke Zarathustra, it responds to the collapse of inherited moral certainties: with old sources of meaning discredited, Nietzsche imagines a figure who affirms life and legislates new purposes for existence. It is an ideal or aspiration rather than a biological type, and Nietzsche presents it as the goal humanity might set for itself once it stops looking beyond this world for value.
eternal-recurrence: Eternal recurrence is Nietzsche's thought that one's life, and indeed the whole of existence, repeats identically an infinite number of times. He offers it less as a cosmological claim than as a test of one's attitude toward life: could you will to live this same life, with all its pain and triviality, over and over forever? To embrace the prospect joyfully rather than with despair is, for Nietzsche, the mark of a life fully affirmed, and the idea is closely tied to his call to love existence exactly as it is.
amor-fati: Amor fati, Latin for "love of fate," is Nietzsche's formula for the highest affirmation of life: not merely to endure what happens but to love it, wanting nothing to be different in the past, present, or future. It stands opposed to resentment and to the wish that reality were other than it is, treating even suffering and necessity as things to be embraced rather than merely tolerated. Nietzsche presents this loving acceptance of one's whole existence as a sign of psychological greatness and a companion to his idea of eternal recurrence.
master-slave-morality: In On the Genealogy of Morality, Nietzsche distinguishes two contrasting sources of moral valuation. Master morality arises among the strong and self-affirming, who call their own qualities "good" and see weakness as merely "bad"; slave morality arises among the oppressed and resentful, who first brand the powerful as "evil" and then define themselves as "good" by contrast. Nietzsche argues that much of modern Western morality, especially values like humility and pity, descends from this reactive slave revolt in ethics, and he uses the distinction to question the origins and worth of our inherited moral concepts.
death-of-god: "God is dead" is Nietzsche's diagnosis, most famously voiced by a madman in The Gay Science, that belief in the Christian God and the moral and metaphysical order it underwrote has lost its hold on Western culture. He does not mean it as a triumphant slogan but as an event of enormous consequence: without a divine guarantor of meaning and value, humanity risks sliding into nihilism unless it can create new values for itself. The phrase names both a cultural crisis and an opportunity, marking the loss of an absolute foundation and the task of finding meaning without one.
nietzsche-perspectivism: Perspectivism is Nietzsche's view that there is no purely objective, view-from-nowhere knowledge; all seeing and knowing occurs from some particular standpoint shaped by interests, drives, and circumstances. Rather than concluding that anything goes, he suggests that understanding grows by drawing on many perspectives, since the more angles we bring to bear on a matter, the more complete our grasp of it becomes. The idea challenges the notion of a single absolute truth and treats our concepts and values as interpretations rather than neutral mirrors of reality.
apollonian-dionysian: In The Birth of Tragedy, Nietzsche describes two artistic and psychological impulses through Greek mythological figures. The Apollonian, named for Apollo, stands for order, clarity, individuation, form, and the beauty of measured appearance; the Dionysian, named for Dionysus, stands for ecstasy, intoxication, dissolution of the self, and the chaotic vitality beneath appearances. Nietzsche argues that Greek tragedy achieved greatness by fusing the two, and he uses the pair more broadly to analyze the tension between rational form and elemental energy in art and life.
ressentiment: Ressentiment, a French term Nietzsche adopts, names a smoldering resentment felt by those who are powerless to act on their hostility and instead turn it inward, reimagining their weakness as virtue. In his account of the origins of morality, this reactive feeling drives the "slave revolt" in ethics: unable to triumph directly, the aggrieved condemn the strong as evil and elevate meekness and restraint into moral ideals. Nietzsche treats ressentiment as a psychological engine that quietly reshapes values, generating morality from frustrated hostility rather than from strength.
last-man: The Last Man is Nietzsche's satirical portrait, drawn in Thus Spoke Zarathustra, of a degraded end-state of humanity: a comfort-seeking creature who has abandoned all high aspiration, striving, and risk in favor of safety, mild pleasure, and contentment. Blinking complacently, the last man asks "What is love? What is creation?" and no longer understands the questions. Nietzsche presents this figure as the opposite of the Übermensch and as a warning about a culture that, having lost its ideals, settles into shallow self-satisfaction.
marx-alienation: Alienation is Karl Marx's term for the estrangement workers experience under capitalist production, developed especially in his early Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts. Because laborers do not own what they make and sell their activity for wages, Marx argues they become separated from the products of their work, from the act of laboring itself, from their own human potential, and from one another. Work, which should express human creativity, instead becomes an external compulsion, and the theory grounds Marx's critique of how capitalism distorts human life.
commodity-fetishism: Commodity fetishism is the concept, introduced in the first volume of Capital, that under capitalism the social relations between people take on the appearance of relations between things. Goods seem to possess value as a natural property of their own, obscuring the human labor and social arrangements that actually produced them. Marx uses the religious language of "fetishism" to capture how market exchange makes economic relations look like objective facts about objects, mystifying the labor that lies behind prices and commodities.
historical-materialism: Historical materialism is Marx's theory that the fundamental driver of historical change is the way societies organize material production. On this view, the economic base—the forces and relations of production—shapes a society's political institutions, laws, and dominant ideas, and history advances through transformations in these material conditions and the class conflicts they generate. Developed with Friedrich Engels, it reframes history not as a story of ideas alone but as a succession of modes of production, each carrying the tensions that eventually give rise to the next.
class-struggle: Class struggle is Marx and Engels's claim, announced in the opening of The Communist Manifesto, that the history of society is a history of conflict between classes with opposing economic interests. In capitalism this conflict centers on the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat, who must sell their labor to survive. Marx held that this antagonism is built into the structure of production itself and that it would ultimately drive revolutionary change, making class conflict the engine of historical development.
marx-ideology: For Marx, ideology refers to the system of ideas, beliefs, and values that reflects and reinforces the interests of a society's dominant class, often while presenting itself as natural, universal, or simply true. Closely linked is false consciousness, a condition in which subordinate groups misunderstand their real situation and accept beliefs that work against their own interests. Together these concepts explain how prevailing worldviews can obscure exploitation and sustain existing power relations, so that the ruling ideas of an age tend to be the ideas of its ruling class.
social-darwinism: Social Darwinism is the late-nineteenth-century application of biological notions of natural selection and "survival of the fittest" to human societies, economics, and politics. Associated especially with Herbert Spencer, who coined the phrase "survival of the fittest," it held that competition among individuals, groups, or nations was natural and beneficial, and it was often used to justify laissez-faire capitalism, social inequality, and, in some versions, imperialism and racial hierarchy. Widely criticized for confusing description with moral justification, it is now generally regarded as a misuse of evolutionary theory rather than a legitimate extension of it.
